stock_bottles.label: Hydrochloric acid, concentrated
stock_bottles.note: constant-boiling azeotrope 20.2 %; the 37 % strength loses HCl on every opening, so a 1 M made from it is only 1 M 'to 2 %' until standardised against Na2CO3

stock_bottles.label: Sulphuric acid, concentrated
stock_bottles.note: hygroscopic; the bottle gets HEAVIER on the shelf, not lighter

stock_bottles.label: Nitric acid, concentrated
stock_bottles.note: fumes and yellows with light as NO2 dissolves; keep in amber

stock_bottles.label: Ammonia solution 'sp. gr. 0.880'
stock_bottles.note: the 0.880 label is a density, not a concentration - the classic first-year confusion

stock_bottles.label: Sodium hydroxide pellets
stock_bottles.note: assay about 96-98 % with 2-4 % carbonate; a '0.1 M NaOH' made by weighing pellets is wrong until you standardise it and correct for carbonate

stock_bottles.label: Potassium hydrogen phthalate (primary standard)
stock_bottles.note: KHP: 204.22 g/mol, dried at 110 C, standardises NaOH to 0.1 % - the reason NaOH is never a primary standard

stock_bottles.label: Anhydrous sodium carbonate (primary standard)
stock_bottles.note: 105.99 g/mol, dry at 270-300 C not above (it starts losing CO2); the acidimetric standard

stock_bottles.label: Oxalic acid dihydrate
stock_bottles.note: 126.07 g/mol; can be weighed directly, unlike KMnO4 - so it is the standard that standards permanganate

stock_bottles.label: Sodium thiosulphate pentahydrate
stock_bottles.note: 248.18 g/mol; the crystals effloresce, so make it in boiled-and-cooled water with a pinch of Na2CO3 and standardise after a week

stock_bottles.label: Potassium permanganate
stock_bottles.note: never a primary standard - it always carries MnO2, which photodecomposes more of it; boil, keep 2 days in the dark, filter through glass wool, then standardise on oxalate

stock_bottles.label: Silver nitrate, 0.05 M
stock_bottles.note: 8.4935 g/L; amber bottle; it stains skin black because light reduces it to silver metal

stock_bottles.label: EDTA disodium dihydrate, 0.01 M
stock_bottles.note: 3.7224 g/L; can be made by weighing directly (a genuine primary standard for complexometry)

stock_bottles.label: Sulphuric acid 1 M (for permanganate work)
stock_bottles.note: always acidify with H2SO4 - HCl is oxidised by permanganate and HNO3 pre-oxidises your Fe2+

stock_bottles.label: Universal indicator solution
stock_bottles.note: about 0.04 % each of methyl orange, methyl red, bromothymol blue and phenolphthalein in ethanol/water - that is why the sequence of colours is what it is

stock_bottles.label: Phenolphthalein indicator
stock_bottles.note: 1 % w/v in 50 % ethanol; two drops per 100 mL; a pink that fades within 30 s means the CO2 of the air got in - a real, common 'failed end point'

stock_bottles.label: Methyl orange indicator
stock_bottles.note: 0.1 % in water; do not use it for a weak-acid titration - its range (3.1-4.4) is nowhere near the basic end point

stock_bottles.label: Lime water, saturated
stock_bottles.note: about 1.7 g/L at 20 C and LESS as it warms (retrograde solubility); a fresh solution must be decanted off the crust, and it never lasts more than a week open

stock_bottles.label: Barium chloride solution, 5 %
stock_bottles.note: the sulphate reagent; acidify the test solution with dilute HCl first or a sulphite/carbonate false-positive appears

stock_bottles.label: Hydrogen peroxide 20 volume
stock_bottles.note: '20 volume' means 20 L of O2 from 1 L of solution; ~1.94 M and it halves in activity in a warm cupboard in a month

stock_bottles.label: Bromine water, saturated
stock_bottles.note: shake liquid bromine with water; the aqueous layer is decanted - and this bottle must be stoppered and kept cool or the lab smells for a week

stock_bottles.label: Iodine solution (Lugol)
stock_bottles.note: 5 g I2 + 10 g KI per 100 mL; the KI is not a catalyst, it is the solvent (I3-); amber bottle

stock_bottles.label: Sodium sulphite solution (fresh)
stock_bottles.note: make from the solid just before use; on air it becomes sulphate and the SO2 generation stops working, which is the #1 'my reagent is dead' report

stock_bottles.label: Tollens' reagent (make fresh, use at once)
stock_bottles.note: to 2 mL of 0.05 M AgNO3 add NaOH to precipitate the oxide, then NH3 dropwise just until it dissolves; NEVER store - ammoniacal silver deposits explosive Ag3N on standing

stock_bottles.label: Fehling's A and B
stock_bottles.note: A: 34.6 g/L CuSO4.5H2O. B: 173 g/L potassium sodium tartrate + 70 g/L NaOH. Mix equal volumes at the moment of use - that is why it is two bottles

stock_bottles.label: Benedict's reagent
stock_bottles.note: 17.3 g/L CuSO4.5H2O + 100 g/L sodium carbonate + 173 g/L sodium citrate; alkaline citrate instead of tartrate, so it is stable and can be stored in one bottle

stock_bottles.label: Soda lime
stock_bottles.note: NaOH about 4 % + CaO 94 % with a water indicator; absorbs CO2 and dries; the CO2 absorbent of every respiration experiment

stock_bottles.label: Silica gel, blue indicating
stock_bottles.note: CoCl2-doped; regenerate at 120 C until blue; about 5 g of gel takes up ~1 mL of water

stock_bottles.label: Concentrated hydrochloric acid, 2 M (working)
stock_bottles.note: dilute the concentrated bottle 1:6, not 1:5 - the arithmetic students get wrong is the dilution factor, not the equation

indicators.name: Thymol blue (1st range)
indicators.note: for strong acid against carbonate-free base

indicators.name: Methyl orange
indicators.note: strong acid vs weak base (NH4OH); NOT for acetic acid vs NaOH

indicators.name: Bromophenol blue
indicators.note: cheap and sharp

indicators.name: Methyl red
indicators.note: the best single indicator for a weak acid titrated with a strong base only if you correct for the 0.1 pH shift

indicators.name: Litmus
indicators.note: the teaching indicator; useless for precision, superb for 'is it acidic at all'

indicators.name: Bromothymol blue
indicators.note: the neutral-range indicator; for CO2-in-water and respiration experiments

indicators.name: Phenol red
indicators.note: cell-culture medium colour; the same chemistry as the milk-souring demo

indicators.name: Neutral red
indicators.note: vital stain in biology, so a shared bottle between departments

indicators.name: Naphtholphthalein
indicators.note: sharper than phenolphthalein for carbonate titrations

indicators.name: Phenolphthalein
indicators.note: the standard for weak acid/strong base; in >12 M base the pink FADES to colourless (carbinol) - an observation that has wasted a thousand student hours

indicators.name: Thymolphthalein
indicators.note: for carbonate-free hydroxide titrations

indicators.name: Alizarin yellow R
indicators.note: the only usable one above pH 11

indicators.name: Eriochrome Black T
indicators.note: complexometric: the metal-indicator complex is wine red and EDTA steals the metal to give blue; needs pH 10 buffer

indicators.name: Murexide
indicators.note: calcium at pH 12 (the Mg is already precipitated and cannot interfere)

indicators.name: Calcon / Eriochrome Blue Black R
indicators.note: calcium with EDTA at high pH

indicators.name: Fluorescein (adsorption indicator)
indicators.note: Fajans chloride titration - the precipitate surface changes colour, not the solution

indicators.name: Potassium chromate (Mohr)
indicators.note: not a pH indicator at all: it is the end-point PRECIPITATE for AgNO3 vs chloride

indicators.name: Diphenylamine
indicators.note: redox (dichromate/permanganate) in sulfuric acid; destroyed by excess oxidiser, so add it in excess too

indicators.name: Ferroin
indicators.note: the Ce4+/Fe2+ and dichromate titration indicator; E0' = 1.06 V

indicators.name: Starch
indicators.note: with I2/I3- only; add near the end point of an iodine titration - too early the complex is slow to release iodine and you overshoot; hot starch stops working

paper_tests.name: red litmus
paper_tests.how: dip or touch with a glass rod
paper_tests.note: the only test a beginner needs for a base

paper_tests.name: blue litmus
paper_tests.note: and for ammonia gas it must be DAMP

paper_tests.name: universal / pH paper
paper_tests.how: touch, do not dip into the sample
paper_tests.positive: 0.5-1 pH unit; a dipped strip leaches dye into your solution
paper_tests.note: for quantitative work use a meter; for 'is it 2 or is it 6' the paper is faster

paper_tests.name: starch-iodide paper
paper_tests.how: hold at the mouth of the tube, or wet it and use as a spot plate
paper_tests.positive: blue-black with any oxidiser that frees iodine: Cl2, Br2, NO2, O3, H2O2, Fe3+, MnO4-, NO2-
paper_tests.note: a positive does NOT mean chlorine - that is the exam trap

paper_tests.name: lead acetate paper
paper_tests.how: hang at the mouth of the reaction vessel
paper_tests.positive: brown to black with H2S or any soluble sulphide
paper_tests.note: and the black stain can be 'restored' by a drop of H2O2 (PbS -> PbSO4), a nice self-check

paper_tests.name: acidified potassium dichromate paper
paper_tests.positive: orange to green with a reducing gas (SO2, H2S)
paper_tests.note: the discriminator between SO2 and CO2, which limewater cannot separate

paper_tests.name: magnesium oxide / 'burning splint'
paper_tests.positive: relights for O2; extinguishes for CO2 and N2
paper_tests.note: and NO browns at the mouth - always note WHICH of these you used

paper_tests.name: cobalt chloride paper
paper_tests.how: dry, and kept in a stoppered tube
paper_tests.note: the water test that is not copper sulphate, and it regenerates in a warm oven

paper_tests.name: turmeric paper
paper_tests.positive: brown to red-brown with a borate; the colour goes green with ammonia fumes
paper_tests.note: rosocyanine - the only borate test that needs no special reagent

paper_tests.name: ginger/guaiac paper
paper_tests.note: old-fashioned but a real enzyme demonstration

group 0 (ammonium).reagent: NaOH solution, warm; then Nessler's reagent on a spot
group 0 (ammonium).gas: NH3 (pungent, turns damp red litmus blue, white fumes with HCl)
group 0 (ammonium).why: must come FIRST because every later group reagent is ammoniacal - a solution that was never tested for NH4+ cannot be reported as NH4+-free

group I (lead, mercury(I), silver).reagent: dilute HCl, cold, in the presence of a little excess acid

precipitate.PbCl2: white needles, soluble in hot water
precipitate.AgCl: white curdy, soluble in NH3 then reprecipitated by HNO3

group I (lead, mercury(I), silver).why: Ksp: AgCl 1.8e-10, PbCl2 1.7e-5 (but 3x more soluble hot), Hg2Cl2 1.4e-18 - the only chlorides that are insoluble enough to fall in 0.3 M HCl
group I (lead, mercury(I), silver).separation: boil the residue with water: PbCl2 dissolves (confirm with K2CrO4 -> yellow PbCrO4); the residue goes to NH3 for silver vs mercury
group I (lead, mercury(I), silver).gotcha: an excess of HCl redissolves PbCl2 as [PbCl4]2-, and too little HCl leaves BiOCl/SbOCl basic salts which look exactly like a group-I precipitate

group II (Cu, Cd, Bi, Hg, As, Sb, Sn).reagent: H2S (or 5 % thioacetamide, 80 C) in 0.3 M HCl
group II (Cu, Cd, Bi, Hg, As, Sb, Sn).why: in 0.3 M acid [S2-] is about 1e-22 M, so Q exceeds Ksp only for the truly insoluble sulphides - ZnS (2e-25), MnS, NiS, CoS all stay in solution
group II (Cu, Cd, Bi, Hg, As, Sb, Sn).separation: IIA dissolves in yellow ammonium polysulphide (As, Sb, Sn thio-salts); IIB (Cu, Cd, Bi, Pb, Hg) does not
group II (Cu, Cd, Bi, Hg, As, Sb, Sn).gotcha: the classic error is adding the H2S before the acid, so zinc and nickel come down with everything and the whole scheme collapses

group III (Fe, Al, Cr).reagent: NH4Cl (solid, dissolved) then NH4OH to ammonia smell, warm
group III (Fe, Al, Cr).why: the buffer holds [OH-] near 1e-5 M: enough for Al(OH)3 (3e-34) and Fe(OH)3 (2.8e-39) to precipitate quantitatively but not Mg(OH)2 (5.6e-12), and Zn/Ni/Co stay as their ammine complexes
group III (Fe, Al, Cr).separation: dissolve the residue in NaOH: Al(OH)3 and Cr(OH)3 go into solution (aluminate, chromite), Fe(OH)3 does not - the split
group III (Fe, Al, Cr).gotcha: if you skip NH4Cl the OH- is high enough that magnesium precipitates too; and any phosphate present drags everything down as phosphates

group IV (Zn, Mn, Ni, Co).reagent: H2S in ammoniacal solution (after group III is filtered off)
group IV (Zn, Mn, Ni, Co).why: at pH 9 [S2-] rises by about ten orders of magnitude, so the more soluble sulphides can now exceed their Ksp - the SAME reagent as group II, only a different pH, which is the entire teaching value of this scheme
group IV (Zn, Mn, Ni, Co).separation: dissolve in dilute HCl (ZnS, MnS dissolve; NiS/CoS, once 'aged', refuse) and re-precipitate
group IV (Zn, Mn, Ni, Co).gotcha: NiS and CoS go 'insoluble' if they are boiled too long - the old saying 'a precipitate that has aged is a precipitate you cannot redissolve' is a real crystallographic ageing effect, not superstition

group V (Ba, Sr, Ca).why: carbonates of the alkaline earths are all far below Ksp; magnesium stays because MgCO3 needs higher [CO3^2-] and MgNH4PO4 needs phosphate, absent here
group V (Ba, Sr, Ca).separation: acetic acid dissolves all three; then K2CrO4 precipitates Ba (yellow BaCrO4, insoluble in acetic acid), NH4OH reprecipitates Sr and Ca... standard split: Ba with chromate, Sr with CaSO4/acetone, Ca with ammonium oxalate
group V (Ba, Sr, Ca).gotcha: if phosphate was not removed at group III the whole group V is a false positive

precipitate.MgNH4PO4: white crystalline with sodium phosphate + NH3

group VI (Mg, Na, K, NH4 leftover).why: sodium and potassium have no common insoluble salt worth precipitating, so these are flame and specific-reagent ions

confirm.Mg2+: white ppt with Na2HPO4 in ammoniacal solution
confirm.Na+: persistent yellow flame; uranyl magnesium acetate -> pale yellow crystals
confirm.K+: lilac flame through cobalt glass; sodium cobaltinitrite -> yellow ppt

dilute H2SO4 tests.carbonate: brisk effervescence, gas clouds limewater (and the milkiness redissolves on excess)
dilute H2SO4 tests.sulphite: pungent SO2, decolourises acidified KMnO4 and turns dichromate paper green
dilute H2SO4 tests.sulphide: rotten-egg gas, blackens lead acetate paper
dilute H2SO4 tests.nitrate: nothing cold; on warming with Cu turnings, brown NO2 fumes
dilute H2SO4 tests.halide: HCl: white fumes only; HBr: orange-brown Br2 (acid fumes); HI: violet I2 plus black solid and H2S smell
dilute H2SO4 tests.acetate: the ester smell with a drop of ethanol and warm acid

concentrated H2SO4 + MnO2 / dry tests.nitrate: brown NO2 with concentrated H2SO4 on the solid, and the brown ring with FeSO4
concentrated H2SO4 + MnO2 / dry tests.chloride: greenish-yellow Cl2 which whitens starch-iodide paper
concentrated H2SO4 + MnO2 / dry tests.iodide: violet vapour; plus H2S and the black solid - iodide reduces the acid
concentrated H2SO4 + MnO2 / dry tests.oxalate: CO and CO2 - the gas burns blue and clouds limewater
concentrated H2SO4 + MnO2 / dry tests.tartrate: the burnt-sugar smell of pyruvic aldehyde
concentrated H2SO4 + MnO2 / dry tests.borate: the green-edged flame with ethanol and acid (turmeric test as backup)

solution tests.sulphate: white BaSO4, insoluble in concentrated HCl
solution tests.phosphate: yellow (NH4)3PO4.12MoO3 with ammonium molybdate in HNO3, on warming
solution tests.chromate/dichromate: yellow with Ba2+ in neutral; the acidified dichromate + H2O2/ether blue (CrO5) is the specific test
solution tests.thiosulphate: acid gives a yellow sulfur cloud + SO2 smell; and it decolourises iodine without the starch colour ever appearing
solution tests.fluoride: etches glass - the only school-relevant 'test' that destroys its own apparatus, so the sim runs it as the 'silicic acid' tube
solution tests.iodide: blue-black with chloramine-water in the right excess (the Schumberger test)
solution tests.bromide/iodide (after the group): chloroform layer colours after adding chlorine water in excess: bromine orange -> iodine violet -> colourless as the iodine is oxidised to iodate

organic_tests.caution: phenols, anilines, aldehydes and enols also decolourise - so run it with the litmus test for HBr
same interferences; formic acid, SO2 and reducing sugars all respond
the carbon percentage is the explanation; not a specific test

organic_tests.positive: AgX curds: white (Cl), cream (Br), yellow (I); rate: tertiary > secondary > primary
organic_tests.caution: the rate IS the mechanism (SN1) - the app should let the student predict before it runs

organic_tests.positive: cloudiness: tertiary at once, secondary 5 min, primary none
organic_tests.caution: only valid for C<=6 alcohols; longer chains are insoluble anyway and look 'positive'
tertiary alcohols give nothing, which is the classification; aldehydes and phenols also reduce it
glycerol, sugars, tartarate all positive - a 'multiple OH on adjacent carbons' test

organic_tests.reagent: Tollens' reagent, warm in a water bath
organic_tests.caution: reducing sugars, formic acid, alpha-hydroxy ketones are also positive; the reagent must be made and destroyed the same day
ketoses are positive too (enediol rearrangement) - which is the most commonly mis-taught 'specific' test in chemistry
SO2 gives a false magenta that acid destroys; formalin gives a blue-white product, not magenta

organic_tests.positive: yellow CHI3 flakes with an antiseptic smell
organic_tests.caution: acetaldehyde, propan-2-ol, lactic acid and pyruvic acid all positive - it tests CH3CO-, not a functional group
the one clear difference from phenol; stronger-than-carbonic acids only
and the ester smell with ethanol and a drop of acid confirms it
the general test for esters and anhydrides, far better than the smell
enols and some carboxylates colour too; and salicylic acid gives violet-red, aspirin nothing - the reaction that grades your own synthesis
far more sensitive than litmus for phenol in water

organic_tests.positive: the most unpleasant smell in the syllabus

halogenated organic.rule: never down the drain; a separate labelled drum - incineration is the only route
halogenated organic.why: ozone-depleting and/or persistent, and they partition into your body fat

non-halogenated organic.rule: flammable-solvent waste drum, no more than 5 L in the room, away from oxidisers
non-halogenated organic.why: vapour heavier than air travels to a flame across the floor

heavy metal (Cr, Pb, Cd, Hg, Ba).rule: collect, never pour out; a licensed carrier; soluble barium and all chromium(VI) are the acute ones
heavy metal (Cr, Pb, Cd, Hg, Ba).why: Pb/Cd/Hg are cumulative; Cr(VI) is a carcinogen by inhalation and a corrosive by contact

cyanide / sulfide residues.rule: keep alkaline, never mix with acid waste, hand to the collector
cyanide / sulfide residues.why: acid contact releases HCN or H2S in the waste bottle itself

acids and alkalis (aqueous).rule: dilute to under 1 M and flush with 20 volumes of water only where local rules allow; otherwise neutralise to pH 6-8 with carbonate, not with the other concentrated bottle
acids and alkalis (aqueous).why: the heat of neutralisation in a small waste jug can crack it

oxidiser solids (permanganate, dichromat.rule: keep in a labelled jar, never in a drawer with organics, no paper padding
oxidiser solids (permanganate, dichromat.why: the oxidiser waste incident is the most common serious lab fire

broken glass / sharps.rule: rigid box, not the bin; pipettes tip-first
broken glass / sharps.why: the injury is in the bin bag, not in the beaker

reactive metals (Na, K, Li, Mg powder, A.rule: quench by dissolving in isopropanol, then ethanol, then water - in that order, outdoors
reactive metals (Na, K, Li, Mg powder, A.why: dropping sodium into water is the funniest thing until the piece is bigger than you thought

mercury spill.rule: ventilate, collect beads with card + tape or zinc foil/amalgam, dust with sulfur, never a vacuum cleaner, never a floor drain
mercury spill.why: the vapour is the poison and a vacuum is a mercury-vapour generator

storage_rules.why: acids together, but nitric acid on its own shelf - nitric fumes attack every other bottle and can start a fire in an organic one
solvents only, metal bin, no fridge unless it is an explosion-rated one (a domestic fridge has a spark every time the thermostat cycles)
away from any fuel and from the acid cabinet; ammonium nitrate and permanganate not in the same cupboard
AgNO3, Hg2(NO3)2, KMnO4, H2O2 (vented cap), chlorine water, Fe(III) oxalate
NaOH, KOH, CaCl2, P2O5, conc H2SO4, CaO - all with tight caps and dated
ammonia separate from acids across the room, not on the same shelf - the white NH4Cl dust will cover everything
chained upright, cap on when not in use, fuel gas and oxygen separated by a distance or a barrier
nothing volatile and nothing food-labelled in the same fridge as anything you intend to eat

emergency.acid or alkali in the eye: Immediately at the eye wash: hold the lids open with your fingers, flush for a FULL 15 minutes, then a doctor. Neutralising is wrong - it adds a second burn and heat. Blink while flushing and move the eye side to side.
emergency.acid on the skin: Flood with water for 15-20 minutes while removing clothing/jewellery. For hydrofluoric acid: keep flushing and get calcium gluconate gel on it, then an emergency department even if it does not hurt yet (HF burns are delayed by hours and destroy bone).
emergency.phenol on the skin: Do not just use water - phenol is only sparingly soluble. Wash with PEG 300 or glycerol, then lots of water, then medical attention; it is absorbed and systematically toxic.
emergency.bromine on the skin: Water 15 min, then a paste of glycerol or sodium thiosulphate/bicarbonate; do not cover it airtight.
emergency.alkali burn: Water longer than you think (20 min); the slipperiness is saponified skin, not the alkali itself, so the burn is deeper than it looks.
emergency.mercury spill: Evacuate unnecessary people, open a window, no vacuum, no broom, collect with card/tape, sulfur or zinc-foil afterwards, and put the waste in a sealed jar with water on top.
emergency.fire in a beaker: Cover with a watch glass or beaker larger than it - cut the air. Do NOT carry a burning vessel to a sink. Use a fire blanket, then a CO2/dry-powder extinguisher; sodium and metal fires need dry sand or class-D, never water or CO2.
emergency.solvent fire on a person: Stop, drop and roll, then the blanket; remove contaminated clothing (it keeps burning against skin) and cool the burn with water for 20 min.
emergency.inhalation of fumes: Out into fresh air immediately, sit upright, and for chlorine/phosgene/NO2 even a 'fine' period of a few hours can precede delayed pulmonary oedema - so medical observation is the correct action, not a cup of tea.
emergency.ingestion: Do not induce vomiting for corrosives or hydrocarbons. Rinse mouth, small sips of water, phone the poison centre with the bottle in your hand. Have the label photographed before you need it.
emergency.the glass-cut-and-bleeding-first-aid: Let it bleed a little under running water to flush fragments, no sucking, cover with a dressing and press; a deep hand cut near a tendon needs a surgeon within hours.

Determination of melting point of an org.note: a 1-2 C range means a pure sample; a broad low range means an impurity

Kinetics of the reaction between potassi.note: plot [oxalic] against t; the curve is sigmoid because Mn2+ autocatalyses

Cleaning and polishing a crucible / cons.note: two consecutive weighings within 0.005 g, not 'when it looks dry'

Using a pipette correctly.note: rinse with the solution, fill above the ring, adjust with the forefinger not the thumb, drain and wait 15 s, do NOT blow out the residual drop unless the pipette is marked 'blow'

Filling and reading a burette, removing.note: the bubble in the tip is the most common single source of a 0.3 mL error, which is bigger than the rest of the titration's uncertainty budget

Recording and reporting: concordant titr.note: an app that quietly gives the 'right answer' teaches the wrong skill; this dataset keeps tolerance fields so the app can be honest about error

causes: the burette tip still had an air bubble at the start
you rinsed the conical flask with the analyte (which adds moles)
you read the top of the meniscus for a dark solution and the bottom for a clear one
you waited too long at the end point and the CO2 of the air pulled a phenolphthalein pink back
troubleshooting.fix: the fix: 0.05 mL resolution, same meniscus rule every time, rinse only the burette/pipette with the solution they hold, and swirl while adding, never while looking at the colour

causes: you used too much solvent - a saturated solution hot is not a saturated solution cold if it started dilute
the solution is supersaturated and needs a scratch below the liquid line with a glass rod, or a seed crystal
impurities are holding the crystallisation back
you cooled it too fast and got an oil out instead of crystals
troubleshooting.fix: the fix: evaporate to a smaller volume, scratch, seed, and cool slowly first then in ice

troubleshooting.symptom: the precipitate went through the paper
causes: it was a colloid, not a precipitate - so digest it warm with a little electrolyte
the paper pores were too coarse for the particle size
you filled the cone too high and it went round the edge
troubleshooting.fix: the fix: add a few drops of electrolyte, warm, let it settle, decant first; use a slow/quantitative paper for fine crystalline solids

causes: the product is not dry - the solvent is counted as product
coprecipitated mother liquor (salt) is in it
you weighed the watch glass wrong
troubleshooting.fix: the fix: dry to constant mass and re-weigh; a yield above 100 % is always a measurement problem, never chemistry

causes: the compound stayed dissolved (the classic cold-solvent-misjudgement)
you filtered before it crystallised
you used an old reagent: Na2SO3, H2O2, Na2S2O3 and SnCl2 all fail silently
troubleshooting.fix: the fix: check the solubility at the temperature you actually reached; test your reagent on a known sample first

troubleshooting.symptom: the pH meter drifts and jumps
causes: the bulb is dirty or dried out
the reference junction is blocked so the circuit is intermittent
the buffer solutions are old or the bottle was cross-contaminated
the temperature was not compensated
troubleshooting.fix: the fix: store the bulb in KCl solution not distilled water, calibrate fresh each session (two points bracketing your sample), and rinse between samples with the sample itself for a cheap probe

troubleshooting.symptom: your electrochemistry reading is far from the textbook EMF
causes: junction and internal resistance (a school voltmeter loads the cell)
the concentrations are not 1 M and you did not use Nernst
the electrodes are oxidised (Al, Zn, Fe all carry films)
polarisation/bubbles on an electrode
troubleshooting.fix: the fix: use a high-impedance digital meter, clean the metals with emery, and compute the expected value at your actual concentrations - then the residual is overpotential, which is a real number worth reporting

troubleshooting.symptom: the gas collected over water gave the wrong moles
causes: you forgot the aqueous tension (about 2.4 kPa at 20 C, i.e. 2.4 % of an atmosphere)
you read the volume with the water levels unequal inside and outside (a few cm of water = a few percent)
the gas is soluble in water (NH3, HCl, SO2, CO2 partly) and never should have been collected this way
the apparatus leaked while cooling, and the syringe/friction offset the reading
troubleshooting.fix: the fix: subtract vapour pressure, match levels, rock the syringe plunger before reading, and choose the collection method from the gas's own properties

troubleshooting.symptom: the flame test was yellow no matter what
causes: sodium is on everything - your hands, the water, the glass, the wire
the nichrome loop was not clean
the sample solution was concentrated to a degree that washes everything out
troubleshooting.fix: the fix: clean the loop in HCl until it burns colourless, use distilled water, and look through cobalt glass for potassium

troubleshooting.symptom: your enthalpy number was too small
causes: you ignored the calorimeter's own heat capacity (a glass beaker holds about as much heat as 60-100 mL of water)
the reaction was slow and the heat leaked away while it ran
the acid/base was not the concentration you thought
for combustion: incomplete burning shows as soot, and the soot IS your missing enthalpy
troubleshooting.fix: the fix: add the water equivalent of the vessel, plot temperature against time and extrapolate to the mixing moment, and use a lid

weak_acid_ph.basis: [H+] solved from Ka and 0.1 M, i.e. the approximation the engine must NOT rely on - the quadratic is used

entries.note: three usable protons, third too weak to titrate
apparent (includes dissolved CO2); true H2CO3 pKa1 = 6.35
SO2.H2O; often quoted 1.81/7.00 depending on convention
weak because of ion pairing, not because of bond strength alone
2nd pKa is contested (12-19 in literature); school value 14
glycolic - the alpha-OH pulls pKa down
chloral hydrate - the strongest 'alcohol' in the list
= pKw at 25 C, used as the reference for OH- acids
ascorbic - the 4.10 is the enediol OH
Lewis acid (accepts OH-), not a Bronsted donor
anilinium - why aniline is a weak base
methylammonium - aliphatic amines are much stronger bases
urea N-H; its conjugate acid pKa is 0.18
hypochlorous - which is why bleach is alkaline and stings as an acid
nitrous; older books say 3.15 - the difference changes the diazotisation calc barely
permanganic acid is strong, which is why KMnO4 solutions are neutral
arsenious (as the acid, not the base)
hydrated Fe3+ is an acid - the reason FeCl3 solution has pH about 2
same story for aluminium, and why alum water is acidic
weak; the reason 'copper sulphate solution is faintly acidic'

safety_index.rule: an app-level guard must be: refuse if the reaction is in reactions_hard_stopped, or if a reagent is in species_hazard5 and the user has no hood; warn otherwise. The refusal text comes from lab.refusals, so the app never argues with the user - it quotes.
